leading_positions.synthesis: Both supporters prefer the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, citing completion of the Standard Model, full maturity, and the fact that the 2013 prize covered the theory. They differ on laureates: Danielsson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, Pearce proposes Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee. They also differ in emphasis, with Danielsson stressing conception and leadership at the time of the announcement and Pearce stressing construction of the detectors. Both concede that three names cannot represent two collaborations of thousands. Pearce (the Chair) is one of the two supporters and has disclosed an instrumentalist bias, so this entry should not be read as carrying any special weight.

Both supporters prefer magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, and both use the same theory-then-experiment argument (2011 prediction, 2018 observation, broad replication). Both also name the same weaknesses: the unsettled pairing mechanism, sample dependence, and the absence of first-author experimentalists and device groups (Cao, Dean) from the credited names. They draw the same conclusion on the three-name credit. They differ in how heavily they weigh the attribution gap: Eriksson says it weakens the case for a prize this year, while Olsson regards the credit as defensible if the citation is built around the discovery.

Both supporters prefer quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, citing the Mott transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopy, and more than twenty years of replication. They share Bloch and Greiner but split on the third name: Mehlig proposes Esslinger and an experiment-only prize, while Johansson proposes Zoller and a mixed theory-plus-experiment prize, having moved from B011 in round 1. Their citations therefore describe different prizes. Both agree that the five-to-three cut is the main weakness and that Cirac and Zoller should not be rewarded twice across B001 and B011.

Both supporters prefer optical lattice clocks with Katori and Ye, the only two-name credit on the shortlist, and both treat the control of systematics at 10^-18 as the substance of the achievement. Their citations are close: Kroll runs from the magic-wavelength concept to its realisation, Lindroth stresses invention plus control of shifts. They share the same reservation, that this may be read as precision metrology rather than discovery and that other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups are outside the credit. Kroll moved here from B003 after reading round 1; Lindroth held her first-round position.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members stated a single-ballot preferred configuration, and the eight positions fall into four pairs (B020, B041, B001, B013) with two explicit supporters each; no ballot has more than two.

No member disputes the scientific quality of the Higgs discovery, the optical-lattice work, magic-angle graphene or the lattice clocks; the disagreements are about attribution, maturity and ranking between them.
Members across all four camps identify the three-person limit as the central difficulty for B020 (four credited names, two collaborations) and for B001 (five credited names).
Several members, including Johansson, Kroll, Mehlig and Pearce, state that B001 and B011 should not both be rewarded with the same people, so they treat them as one family of cases.

B001 is named as a first or second alternative by Danielsson, Eriksson, Kroll, Olsson, Pearce and Lindroth, and Mehlig and Johansson prefer it outright; B013 and B041 also recur as alternatives. This is a count of explicit alternatives in the round-1 files only.
scientific_disputes: Whether the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene should count against B041 (Danielsson, Mehlig, Johansson) or whether the discovery of flat-band correlated states is robust whatever the mechanism (Eriksson, Olsson).
Whether optical lattice clocks (B013) are a discovery or a precision-measurement advance building on the 2005 comb prize (raised by Kroll and Lindroth themselves and by Johansson).
Whether analogue quantum simulation in B001 has yet produced new physics or mainly demonstrated capability on known models (Mehlig, Lindroth, Johansson on prospects of quantum advantage).
Whether the Higgs discovery is sufficiently distinct from the 2013 prize (Danielsson, Pearce raise it as a risk and judge it distinct).
Whether B003 (Kroll's first choice in the opening ballot) is a single discovery or a compound of cavity QED, memories and network nodes (Johansson, Pearce, Lindroth consider it compound).
attribution_disputes: B020: Danielsson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni; Pearce proposes Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee. The disagreement is whether the prize honours construction and project leadership (favouring Virdee) or leadership at the moment of the announcement (favouring Gianotti). Mehlig, Lindroth, Eriksson, Kroll and Johansson doubt that leadership roles can ground a prize at all.

B001: Bloch and Greiner are common to both proposals, but Mehlig names Esslinger and Johansson names Zoller. Jaksch and Hansch are not on the credited list, and Cirac is excluded from both proposals while appearing in B011.

B041: the same trio is proposed throughout, but Eriksson and Olsson state that early-career experimentalists (Cao) and device groups (Dean) are outside the credited names; they disagree on whether this weakens the case or is an unavoidable consequence of the three-person limit.
B013: Katori and Ye are named by both supporters; Kroll and Lindroth note that other strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups are outside the credit but do not propose changes.
maturity_disputes: B041 is about eight years from the experimental discovery. Eriksson and Olsson regard replication as sufficient; Danielsson, Mehlig and Johansson say that a wait would cost little.
B013: Johansson says the pending redefinition of the second could make recognition early; Kroll says a pending redefinition is evidence of maturity, not a reason to wait.
B003: Pearce and Johansson regard a repeater-based quantum network as not yet realised and the field as insufficiently mature.
B001 is described by Mehlig and Johansson as mature and arguably overdue; Lindroth and Johansson note that quantum advantage has not yet been decisively shown.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson: works in circuit QED and directs WACQT at Chalmers (colleagues Delsing, Wilson); would recuse himself from any decision on B008. He also notes WACQT concerns a platform competing with the Cirac-Zoller proposals.

Kroll: B003 is close to his own optical quantum-memory work and he would recuse himself from it; he also flags, for transparency only, a research stay in John Hall's laboratory (background lineage for B013, no documented link to Katori or Ye).

Lindroth: collaborations in attosecond physics (L'Huillier, Keller, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato), none on B013; she would flag them if the committee turned to the attosecond candidate or to AMO candidates where a collaborator is credited.

Pearce (Chair): no specific conflict for B020; doctoral work in experimental particle physics at Birmingham and CERN, with the experiment not identified in the profile; discloses an instrumentalist preference for detector-driven discovery.
Olsson: notes that Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and that she did not rely on his view of B008.
Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig: no specific conflict identified for any shortlisted entry.
questions_for_round2: B020: can the committee state a principled rule for choosing three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee (construction and conception leadership, or leadership at announcement), and can that rule be written into a citation that names both ATLAS and CMS?

B001: should the prize be experimental only (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger), or mixed with a theory credit (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller)? If mixed, how is Cirac and Zoller's role handled with respect to B011, and how are Jaksch and Hansch accounted for in the background material?

B041: does the committee judge the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and Dean to be a reason to wait, or only an open question inside a durable field? Eriksson and Olsson should address whether the citation can credit the discovery without implying the group leader alone made it.

B013: does the committee view the lattice clock as a discovery or as a measurement advance, and should timing be tied to the redefinition of the second? Do Kroll and Lindroth see any named-credit gap beyond Katori and Ye?

Across the four camps: if no ballot has more than two supporters, which criterion should decide the ranking: maturity, clarity of attribution, or breadth of scientific impact, and how should members who ranked B020 or B013 outside their top three for attribution reasons weigh that against the science?

Can any member propose a two-part configuration that does not reward the same laureates twice or require more than three individuals per part, or is a single-part prize the only feasible output on this shortlist?
summary.chair_observation: The first-round files show four internally consistent camps of two members each, with no ballot able to claim a majority on explicit preferences alone. Each camp's strongest argument is acknowledged as the other camps' main reservation: B020 has the strongest science and the weakest attribution, B041 the cleanest theory-plus-experiment credit but the youngest field, B001 the broadest maturity but a five-to-three cut, and B013 the cleanest two-name credit but the narrowest framing as a discovery. Round 2 should therefore focus on attribution rules and maturity thresholds, not on the quality of the science. As Chair I am a supporter of B020 and have tried to represent the other three positions on their own terms.
